beats.title: Intro: Why a² + b² = c²?
beats.says: Pythagoras' theorem is on almost every GCSE paper. Most people memorise a² plus b² equals c² without ever seeing why it's true. In the next few minutes, you'll see it, and you'll know exactly how to use it.

beats.title: The Picture: The Parts
beats.says: It only works for right-angled triangles. The two shorter sides meet at the right angle. The longest side is opposite the right angle, and it has a special name: the hypotenuse.
beats.onScreen: Triangle diagram: labels, hypotenuse and right angle
beats.key: Hypotenuse = the longest side, opposite the right angle.

beats.title: The Picture: Squares on the Sides
beats.says: Take a triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5, and build a square on each side. The square on the 3 has 9 little squares. The square on the 4 has 16. And the square on the hypotenuse has 25. Look: 9 plus 16 is exactly 25. And it always works.
beats.key: a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse.

beats.title: The Picture: Why It Works
beats.says: Here's why. Put four copies of the triangle inside a big square, one in each corner. The gap left in the middle is a tilted square, and each of its sides is the hypotenuse, so its area is c squared.
beats.onScreen: Proof: four triangles in a big square, the gap is c²

beats.title: The Picture: Slide Them
beats.says: Now slide the triangles around inside the same big square. The gap becomes two squares: a squared and b squared. Same big square, same four triangles, so the gaps must be equal. a squared plus b squared equals c squared.
beats.onScreen: Proof: slide the triangles to leave a² and b²

beats.title: The Method: Finding the Hypotenuse
beats.says: Let's use it. The shorter sides are 6 and 8 centimetres. Find the hypotenuse. Square them: 36 and 64. Add: 100. Then square root: the hypotenuse is 10 centimetres.
beats.onScreen: Triangle diagram: a = 6 cm, b = 8 cm, c = ? | 6² + 8² = c² | 36 + 64 = 100 // square and add | c = √100 = 10 cm // then square root
beats.key: Finding the longest side? Square, add, square root.

beats.title: The Method: Sense Check
beats.says: Quick check: the hypotenuse must be the longest side. 10 is longer than 6 and 8, so that's right. If your answer is shorter, something's gone wrong.
beats.onScreen: Worked: 10 > 8 and 10 > 6 ✓ // the hypotenuse is always the longest | shorter than a side? // you've made a mistake

beats.title: Shorter Side: Subtract
beats.says: If you know the hypotenuse and need a shorter side, you subtract instead. Hypotenuse 13, one side 5. Square them: 169 and 25. Subtract: 144. Square root: the missing side is 12.
beats.onScreen: Triangle diagram: a = ?, b = 5 cm, c = 13 cm | 13² − 5² = a² // the hypotenuse is 13 | 169 − 25 = 144 // square and subtract | a = √144 = 12 cm
beats.key: Finding a shorter side? Square, subtract, square root.

beats.title: Decimals: Rounding
beats.says: Most answers aren't whole numbers. Sides 5 and 7: 25 plus 49 is 74. The square root of 74 is 8.602 and so on, so 8.60 to 2 decimal places. Only round at the very end.
beats.onScreen: Triangle diagram: a = 5 cm, b = 7 cm, c = ? | 5² + 7² = 74 | c = √74 = 8.6023… | c ≈ 8.60 cm // round at the end
beats.key: Round only at the very end.

beats.title: Real Life: The Ladder
beats.says: Exam questions hide triangles in real life. A 5 metre ladder leans against a wall, with its foot 1.5 metres from the wall. How high up does it reach? The ladder is the hypotenuse. 25 minus 2.25 is 22.75, so it reaches about 4.77 metres.
beats.onScreen: Triangle diagram: ladder, a = ?, b = 1.5 m, c = 5 m | 5² − 1.5² = 22.75 // the ladder is the hypotenuse | a = √22.75 ≈ 4.77 m
beats.key: Find the right angle; the side opposite it is the hypotenuse.

beats.title: Coordinates: Distance
beats.says: It also finds the distance between two points. From 1, 2 to 7, 10: that's 6 across and 8 up. Those are the short sides, so the distance is the square root of 36 plus 64, which is 10.
beats.onScreen: Triangle diagram: points (1, 2) and (7, 10) | 6² + 8² = 100 // across 6, up 8 | distance = √100 = 10
beats.key: Distance between points: across and up are the short sides.

beats.title: Exam Tips: Common Mistakes
beats.says: The mistakes that lose marks: adding when you should subtract, because you didn't spot the hypotenuse; forgetting the square root at the end; and rounding too early.
beats.onScreen: Worked: ✗ 13² + 5² // it's a shorter side: subtract | ✗ c = 100 // forgot to square root | ✗ √74 ≈ 8.6, then reused // round at the end | ✓ spot c · square · add or subtract · √

beats.title: Your Turn: Question
beats.says: Your turn. A right-angled triangle has shorter sides of 9 centimetres and 12 centimetres. Find the length of the hypotenuse. Pause the video and try it.
beats.onScreen: Your turn: question card with a countdown. Q: The shorter sides of a right-angled triangle are 9 cm and 12 cm. Find the hypotenuse.
beats.question: The shorter sides of a right-angled triangle are 9 cm and 12 cm. Find the hypotenuse

beats.title: Your Turn: Answer
beats.says: 9 squared is 81, and 12 squared is 144. Add them: 225. The square root of 225 is 15, so the hypotenuse is 15 centimetres. If you got that, you've got it.
beats.onScreen: Your turn: the answer A: c = 15 cm.
beats.question: The shorter sides of a right-angled triangle are 9 cm and 12 cm. Find the hypotenuse
